chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, who said: 'Ja'far (AS) narrated to me from his father (AS) that

Ali (blessings of God be upon him) said: 'Whoever sets himself up for analogy (qiyas) will not cease to be in confusion throughout his lifetime; and whoever makes a religion of God based on personal opinion (ra'y) will not cease to be in a state of drowning throughout his lifetime.'

He said: And Abu Ja'far (AS) said: 'Whoever issues fatwas to the people by his own opinion has thereby made a religion of God with what he does not know; and whoever makes a religion of God with what he does not know has opposed God, making permissible and forbidding that which he does not know.'

key_terms.ارْتِمَاسٍ: irtimas — submersion, drowning; a metaphor for being utterly and irretrievably lost in error
key_terms.الرَّأْيِ: ra'y — personal opinion or rational judgment applied independently in religious matters, without transmitted knowledge from the Imams
key_terms.الْتِبَاسٍ: iltibas — confusion, ambiguity, the perpetual inability to distinguish truth from falsehood
key_terms.الْقِيَاسِ: qiyas — analogical reasoning used to derive rulings; condemned by the Shia Imams as an inadmissible source of religious law

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali (AS) and Imam al-Baqir (AS) say about using personal opinion (ra'y) and analogy (qiyas) to issue religious rulings?
ai.summary: This hadith transmits two closely related condemnations: Imam Ali (AS) declares that those who use qiyas (analogical reasoning) and ra'y (personal opinion) as bases for religion will be perpetually lost in confusion and error. Imam al-Baqir (AS) sharpens the point jurisprudentially — issuing fatwas from personal opinion constitutes 'opposing God,' since the jurist usurps divine authority by permitting and prohibiting matters he has no revealed knowledge of.
